## Current teaching

### Neuro-AI: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Neuroscience {#neuro-ai}

*Seminar.*

Artificial intelligence is reshaping science, medicine, and everyday life. Yet many of its core ideas grew out of a question neuroscience has always asked: what makes a system intelligent? This seminar takes that question as its thread and follows it all the way from the origins of machine learning and AI to the models behind today's most powerful applications. No background is assumed: you start from zero and build upward, step by step, from first principles, so your curiosity matters more than any prior training.

You will trace the history of the field, from its early inspiration in the brain to the deep networks now driving image recognition, language, and scientific discovery, and then open the black box to see how these systems actually work: how a model learns from examples, how it generalises to things it has never seen, and why the very ideas that describe learning in machines also illuminate learning in brains. Concrete stops along the way include the fundamentals of neurons and the visual system, convolutional and generative models for brain imaging, large language models as models of human language, reinforcement learning and reward, and graph networks for brain connectivity. Throughout, you will weigh the bigger questions too: why these advances are changing the world, and what the ethics and hidden biases behind them mean, in humans and machines alike.

The seminar is discussion-driven and hands-on. You read and lead sessions on landmark papers, debate the ideas that matter, and design your own small research proposal that uses AI to tackle a neuroscientific problem, carrying one idea from a first sketch through peer feedback to a written plan. The focus is on intuition and reasoning rather than heavy mathematics, and no programming experience is required. It is meant as a genuine entry point into one of the most exciting frontiers in science today.

Along the way you can explore **[The Intelligence Atlas](https://brain-machines-and-ideas-in-between.vercel.app/en)**, an interactive companion to the course. It lets you follow the ideas that travelled from biological cells to artificial systems and back again: pick a discovery, trace its connections across neuroscience, computation, and machine learning, and see the evidence behind each link, in English, German, or Spanish ([source code](https://github.com/virtualmarioe/brain-machines-and-ideas-in-between), [more on Sci-Comm](sci-comm.qmd#intelligence-atlas)).

### Empirical Research Practicum (EmPra)

*Bachelor's practicum.*

How do we get from seeing a face to knowing a person? In this practicum, you design and run a study on how faces are learned, recognised, and judged, working with photographs of real people alongside faces generated by AI image models. You go through the full empirical cycle: from the literature to a testable hypothesis, then an online experiment, data collection, analysis, and a written report. In small groups you take on complementary questions within one shared design, so the data you collect feed into an ongoing research line of the department. No prior programming experience is expected.
